name: Place de la Bourse
label: Place de la Bourse
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Miroir d'eau' (3 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Miroir d'Eau' (way/53246398): middle (122 m across); moved 15 m off water.
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap relation/1818973: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Place de la Bourse' (158 m across).
notes: 18th-century royal square on the Garonne quays.

text.description:
Place de la Bourse is one of Bordeaux's most recognisable sights, a square of pale 18th-century façades facing the river Garonne. It was built between 1730 and 1775 and designed by Jacques Gabriel and his son Ange-Jacques Gabriel, who finished the work. The Palais de la Bourse stands on the north side, now the Chamber of Commerce and Industry, and the former Hôtel des Fermes on the south side houses the National Museum of Customs. The whole area is part of Bordeaux's UNESCO World Heritage listing, added in 2007.

For a phone photo, the best-known view is from the Miroir d'eau, the shallow pool in front of the Bourse. When the water is calm, the façades are mirrored in a thin sheet of water, which gives a very symmetrical picture. During the mist phase the same buildings appear through rising vapour, which looks especially atmospheric after dark. Early morning is the calmest and least crowded time for the mirror shot.

There are two other views worth trying. One is a low angle from the Quai de la Douane, with the river in the frame. The other is from inside the square itself, with the central fountain in the foreground and the Three Graces sculpture, which dates from 1869.
text.geographic_location: In the historic centre of Bordeaux, beside the river Garonne. The Miroir d'eau pool lies in front of the Bourse, beside the quay.
text.directions_text: Walk from the historic centre of Bordeaux to the riverside, looking for the Garonne and the long row of pale façades. It is about 2 minutes on foot between the two. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the mirrored view, because it keeps the façades looking natural. Switch to the ultra-wide (0.5x) if you cannot fit the whole front and its reflection in. Use the telephoto (2x or more, depending on your phone) for the sculptures and rooflines.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand right at the subject (on the pool, facing the Bourse façades across the water). The 18th-century Bourse façades mirrored in a thin sheet of water when the pool is calm, or the same façades through the rising mist during the cycle. From here the 18th-century buildings are mirrored in a thin sheet of water when the pool is calm, or seen through rising mist during the cycle.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and place the horizon of the water on the lower third line, keeping the central façade in the middle so the reflection looks balanced. Crouch down and hold the phone just above the water for a stronger mirror effect. If you have time, a second angle from the Quai de la Douane gives a low view with the river in the frame.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the façade to focus, then slide the exposure down a little so floodlit stonework does not turn white. After dark, use night mode and brace your elbows against your body, as the mist moves and a sharp shot needs a steady hand. A Live Photo can capture the mist as it rises.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Dusk or blue hour for the floodlit reflection, or early morning for a calm, quiet mirror. One guide says the water cycle runs roughly every 15 to 20 minutes, so wait for the calm phase if you want the mirror.

text.access_note: The square and the Miroir d'eau are open public spaces, though the pool is drained in the coldest winter months and the granite can be slippery when misty, so take care; for the buildings or the museum, check the official site before you go.

name: Cité du Vin
label: La Cité du Vin
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Esplanade de Pontac' (1 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Esplanade de Pontac' (way/416698385): middle (169 m across).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/421965158: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Cité du Vin' (107 m across).
notes: Wine museum in a swirling modern building.

text.description:
The Cité du Vin is Bordeaux's wine museum, and the building is the main reason to photograph it. Its curved, swirling form is often compared to a wine carafe, and it stands right beside the Garonne, so the river gives you a clean backdrop. It was designed by XTU Agency, led by Anouk Legendre and Nicholas Desmazières. It opened to the public on 1 June 2016 and had passed 2 million visitors by May 2022.

The best view of the building itself is from Esplanade de Pontac, the public square in front of the main entrance. From there you see the whole curved silhouette with the river behind it. At low tide, sandbanks show in the water and add something to the foreground, so it is worth glancing at tide times if that appeals.

If you have a little more time, two other views are worth a try. Pont Jacques-Chaban-Delmas gives you the museum across the water, framed against the river. Quai de Bacalan suits close-up shots of the facade and its reflections, or a wider view from the river bank.

The belvedere at the top is a paid visit and gives city views rather than a photo of the building, so it is not part of this shot. Because the building is large and curved, give yourself space and avoid tilting the phone, or the walls will lean.
text.geographic_location: The Cité du Vin stands on the bank of the Garonne in Bordeaux, close to the Pont Jacques-Chaban-Delmas.
text.directions_text: Take line B of the Bordeaux tramway to the Cité du Vin tram stop, which is named after the building. Walk towards the river and the main entrance, and stop on the open square in front of it. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) to fit the full curved building and the river in one frame. Switch to ultra-wide (0.5x) only if you want a dramatic, close-up view, and watch the edges for stretching. Use telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for details of the facade.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand in Esplanade de Pontac (public square in front of the main entrance, facing the building). The building's full curved, wine-carafe silhouette with the Garonne behind it, and sandbanks in the frame at low tide. From here the photo shows the full curved, wine-carafe silhouette with the Garonne behind it, and sandbanks in the frame at low tide.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Switch on gridlines and place the building on one side of the frame, with the river and sky filling the rest. Keep the phone level so the vertical lines do not lean. If you have time, Pont Jacques-Chaban-Delmas gives a view of the museum across the river, and Quai de Bacalan suits close-ups of the facade and its reflections.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the building to focus, then lower the exposure slider slightly so the sky keeps its colour. For reflections on the facade, try the telephoto lens and hold the phone steady with both hands. Use night mode at dusk if the light drops.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Low tide shows sandbanks in the river, which adds to the view from the esplanade, so check tide times. Early or late in the day usually gives softer light on the building.

text.access_note: The esplanade is a free public square, but the belvedere at the top of the building is a paid visit, so check the official site for any other access before you go.

name: Miroir d'eau
label: Miroir d'eau
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Place de la Bourse' (4 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Place de la Bourse' (relation/1818973): middle (158 m across).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/53246398: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Miroir d'Eau' (122 m across).
notes: Reflecting pool facing Place de la Bourse.

text.description:
The Miroir d'eau is a huge, shallow reflecting pool on the Garonne quay, right in front of Place de la Bourse. It covers 3,450 square metres and was built in 2006 to a design by landscape artist Michel Corajoud. The surface is granite slabs under about 2 cm of water. When the water is calm, the 18th-century Bourse façades appear in it almost perfectly, and every 15 minutes a mist rises and softens the whole scene. It is described as the most-photographed place in Bordeaux's Port of the Moon.

The pool photographs well because the square is so symmetrical. The reflection doubles the buildings, and people wading through the water add scale and life. The two phases of the cycle give you two different pictures: sharp reflection, then drifting mist. The reflection is not always there, though. It depends partly on how many people are walking through the water, so be patient and wait for a clear moment. The pool is also only running for part of the year, so check before you travel.

For a phone, the easiest approach is to keep the whole façade in frame, hold the phone low over the water, and take several shots as the cycle changes. Look at the screen before you press the shutter and check that the buildings are not tilted.
text.geographic_location: On the Garonne quay in front of Place de la Bourse, in the old port area of Bordeaux. The river runs along one side of the pool and the Bourse buildings stand on the other.
text.directions_text: Head for Place de la Bourse in the historic centre of Bordeaux. The pool lies between the Bourse façades and the river. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide (0.5x) to fit the full Bourse façades and their reflection in one frame. Switch to the default lens (1x) for a calmer, less stretched view, and use telephoto (2x or more) for details such as people walking through the mist.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand in Place de la Bourse (river (Garonne quay) side of the pool, facing the Bourse façades). The 18th-century Bourse façades reflected in the thin water sheet, with the mist cycle and the square's symmetry framed together. For the full reflection of the Bourse façades, walk to the river (Garonne quay) side of the pool and turn round to face the buildings. From there you can frame the façades, the thin sheet of water and the symmetry of the square together.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and line up the centre of the façade with the middle of the screen so the reflection is balanced. Crouch down and hold the phone just above the water to make the reflection bigger. If you want a different view, the Pont de Pierre gives a more distant picture of the quays and the pool with the river in the foreground, especially once the lights are on.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the buildings to set focus, then drag the exposure slider down a little so the sky does not turn white. Try Live Photos or take a quick burst to catch the mist rising. After dark, use night mode and brace your elbows against your body to keep the phone steady.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early morning, when the water is calm and there are fewer people. Sunset or after dark also works well for lit façades and golden reflections.

text.access_note: This is an open public space beside the quay, but the water mirror only runs for part of the year, so check the official site before you go.
claims_not_in_sources: The Bourse façades stand on the opposite side of the pool from the river, so the pool lies east of the stand-here point on Place de la Bourse.
Walking from the stand-here point to the middle of the pool takes about 2 minutes (calculated from the distance given).
Live Photos or a burst can capture the mist as it rises.
Night mode works better if you hold the phone steady against your body.

name: Grosse Cloche
label: Grosse Cloche
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Cours Victor Hugo' (2 web pages); placed at the stretch of Cours Victor Hugo nearest the subject (our map tiles).
pin_note: Position from OSM W80032457 (Grosse Cloche): kept: no OpenStreetMap object carries this Wikidata ID.
notes: Medieval belfry and gate on Rue Saint-James.

text.description: The Grosse Cloche is an old town gate topped by a bell tower, with a double arch below and a clock face on show. It is a good subject for a phone because the shape is clear and easy to recognise, and you can photograph it in more than one way. From here you see the full front of the gate and the clock face, with more open space around it than in the narrow streets. The tower is set slightly back from this avenue. If you want the classic framed view, walk round to Rue Saint-James. There the double arch and bell tower sit symmetrically between the tall, narrow old-town façades. Place Pey Berland, the open square beside the cathedral, is another option. It is worth checking that view on the day. The bell is said to ring at noon on the first Sunday of the month and on a few special occasions. The street may be busier for a short while then, so allow a little extra time. Inside the tower is a separate guided visit, not an open viewing platform. Take your photos from the street and keep an eye on passing traffic and other people as you step back.
text.geographic_location: In the old town of Bordeaux, on the Cours Victor Hugo side of the gate. Rue Saint-James and Place Pey Berland, beside the cathedral, are other viewpoints for the gate.
text.directions_text: No Underground, train or tram stop is listed for this spot, and it can be reached on foot. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the full front of the gate and the clock face. Switch to the ultra-wide (0.5x) if traffic or people stop you stepping back, but keep the gate away from the edges of the frame, where it can look stretched. Use telephoto (2x or more, depending on your phone) for a tighter shot of the clock face and tower top.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand on Cours Victor Hugo (the view from the Cours Victor Hugo side, where the clock face is visible). The monument seen from the wider boulevard side, including its clock face and the gate's full front. From here the gate lies to the north. You see its full front and the clock face from the wider boulevard side, a more open angle than the narrow-street view.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and line the two sides of the arch up with the vertical lines so the gate stands straight. Leave a little space above the tower so it is not cut off. For a different shot, try Rue Saint-James, where the double arch and bell tower are framed between the old-town façades.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the clock face or the stonework to focus, then slide the exposure down slightly if the sky is bright, so the gate does not turn into a silhouette. Hold the phone with both hands and keep it level.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early morning or late afternoon usually means softer light and fewer people. Avoid noon on the first Sunday of the month if you want a quiet street, when the bell may draw a crowd.

text.access_note: You can photograph the gate from the public street; going inside the tower is a separate guided visit, so check the official site before you go.
claims_not_in_sources: Early morning or late afternoon usually gives softer light and fewer people around the gate.
Ultra-wide lenses can stretch objects near the edges of the frame.
Cours Victor Hugo is a busy road with traffic, so take care when stepping back.

name: Rue Sainte-Catherine
label: Rue Sainte-Catherine
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Place de la Comédie' (2 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Place de la Comédie' (way/23247161): middle (102 m across).
pin_note: Position from the Wikipedia article 'Rue Sainte-Catherine (Bordeaux)'.

text.description:
Rue Sainte-Catherine is the main shopping street of Bordeaux, a pedestrian avenue about 1.2 km long running north to south from the Place de la Comédie to the Place de la Victoire. It follows the line of the old Roman cardo and is often billed as the longest pedestrian street in Europe. It became fully pedestrian in 1984 and was refurbished between 2000 and 2003 in a project by Jean-Michel Wilmotte.

It photographs well because of its length. From the north end, the street runs away between Haussmann-style façades, with shopfronts and people filling the frame and the Grand Théâtre behind you.

Halfway along, Place Saint-Projet has a fountain made around 1715. The street dips into this square, which gives a strong sense of perspective. At the southern end, Place de la Victoire gives a different view, with the shopfronts and pedestrians leading out into the square. Where the street meets the Cours Alsace-Lorraine, look down for a bas-relief marking two underground rivers, the Peugue and the Devèze. Shop entrances are private, so step aside if staff ask. Market days and the sales in February and July can fill the street and block your view.
text.geographic_location: In the historic centre of Bordeaux, running south from Place de la Comédie beside the Grand Théâtre to Place de la Victoire. The Galerie Bordelaise shopping arcade has an entrance at the top of the street.
text.directions_text: Take tram Line B to the Grand Théâtre stop, then walk to Place de la Comédie where the street begins. Line A (Sainte-Catherine stop) and Line B (Victoire stop) also serve the street if you would rather start further along it. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) to show the full length of the street with the Grand Théâtre behind you. Switch to ultra-wide (0.5x) if you want more of the façades, or to telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) to pack the crowd and shopfronts together down the avenue.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand in Place de la Comédie (north end, where the street begins beside the Grand Théâtre). Looking south from the head of the street, the long pedestrian avenue runs away between the Haussmann-style façades, with the Grand Théâtre behind you. On Place de la Comédie, at the north end where the street begins beside the Grand Théâtre. Face south: the long pedestrian avenue runs away between the Haussmann-style façades.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Stand in the middle of the street's line so the façades on both sides lean in evenly towards the far end. If you want a different view, try Place Saint-Projet, where the street slopes into a dip and the crowd recedes in strong perspective. Another option is the southern end at Place de la Victoire, with the street's pedestrians in the frame.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Turn on gridlines and line them up with the façades so the verticals stay straight. Tap on the middle distance to set focus, then nudge the exposure slider down slightly if the sky is bright. A Live Photo can catch the movement of the crowd.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Market days and the sales in February and July can fill the street. One guide suggests evening light falls better down the cross streets than at midday.

text.access_note: This is an open pedestrian street, but shop entrances are private, so step aside if staff ask.
claims_not_in_sources: Walking from the stand-here point to the marked point on the street takes about 5 minutes (309 m x 1.3 / 80 m per minute).

name: Porte Cailhau
label: Porte Cailhau
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Place du Palais' (3 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Place du Palais' (way/193496157): middle (121 m across).
pin_note: Position from Wikidata Q2105012: kept: no OpenStreetMap object carries this Wikidata ID.

text.description:
Porte Cailhau is a late medieval city gate that doubles as a triumphal arch, and it is one of the most recognisable shapes on Bordeaux's skyline. It was built between 1493 and 1496 as part of the old city walls. The walls have gone, but you can still see where they once joined the gate at the back. On the front there is a statue of King Charles VIII, and the gate was partly built to mark his victory at the Battle of Fornovo in 1495. It has been a protected historical monument since 1883 and belongs to the city today.

It photographs well because the front is neat and symmetrical, with a pointed archway, twin turrets and a slate spire. The best frontal view is from across Place du Palais, a pedestrian square named after the Dukes of Aquitaine's palace that stood here until 1791. From there the gate fills the frame without traffic in front of it. Cross to the east side of the gate, into Place du Palais, open the camera app and keep the gate centred so both turrets look even. For a second angle, walk to Quai Richelieu for the whole silhouette with the Garonne and the Pont de Pierre, or try Rue du Quai Bourgeois for a side view with the quayside buildings around it. Going inside the tower is a separate matter, so check the official site before you go.
text.geographic_location: Porte Cailhau stands in the old centre of Bordeaux, at the edge of Place du Palais, a short walk from the Garonne quayside.
text.directions_text: It is about 87 m south-west of the gate, on the river side, and about a minute or two on foot from it. For the frontal view, walk round to Place du Palais on the east side of the gate. If you want the quay view afterwards, walk on towards the river. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) from across Place du Palais so the whole gate fits with some sky above the spire. Use the telephoto (2x to 5x, depending on your phone) for the statue, the turrets and the pointed arch. Use the ultra-wide (0.5x) only if you move close or want the gate with the quayside buildings.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand in Place du Palais (across the square from the town-side (east) façade). The full symmetrical front of the gate, with its pointed archway, twin turrets and slate spire, composed head-on across the pedestrian square. For the classic frontal view, walk round to Place du Palais on the east (town) side and stand across the square from the gate, with the gate to the west of you. From there you see the full symmetrical front, with the pointed archway, twin turrets and slate spire, face-on.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Switch on gridlines and line the archway up with the centre of the frame so the two turrets sit evenly on each side. Hold the phone level, because tilting it makes the tower lean. If you have time, try Quai Richelieu for the silhouette with the Garonne and the Pont de Pierre, or Rue du Quai Bourgeois for a side view in perspective.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the stone façade to set focus, then slide the exposure down a little if the sky is bright, so the sky keeps its colour and the gate stays well exposed. At dusk, try night mode and hold the phone steady against something solid.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early morning, about 7:30 to 9:00 in spring and autumn, when the square is quieter and the light is soft on the façade. A dusk shot from the square or quay is also possible.

text.access_note: The outside of the gate and the square are open public space; going inside the tower is a separate visit, so check the official site before you go.
claims_not_in_sources: Early morning light is soft on the façade and the square is quieter at that time (from the viewpoint research, not from the history sources).
The gate is lit up at night, so a dusk shot is possible (several guides mention floodlighting, but no exact time is given).
Tilting the phone upwards makes the tower appear to lean.

name: Monument aux Girondins
label: Monument aux Girondins
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Place des Quinconces' (3 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Place des Quinconces' (way/351199496): middle (112 m across).
pin_note: Position from OSM W568436009 (Monument aux Girondins): kept: no OpenStreetMap object carries this Wikidata ID.
notes: Column and fountains at the end of Quinconces.

text.description:
The Monument aux Girondins is a tall column topped with a sculpture, rising above a large fountain of bronze horses and other sculptures. It stands in the open space of Place des Quinconces, so it has room around it and trees nearby. The column gives you a strong vertical line, and the fountain below gives you movement and detail.

The classic view is from the north side of the monument, out in the square. Guides say this side shows the fountain and sculptures best, and the horses' lively shapes stand out. The wide open square around you lets you frame the column, the bronze figures and the trees together in one shot.

A few practical points. The fountain does not always have water running; one visitor found it dry. Fairs and events held in the square can also bring crowds or put stalls in the way, so you may need to move a few steps to find a clear angle. For a different picture, the Quai Louis XVIII shows the monument in the distance with the river in the foreground, which suits warm sunset light.

Take a few frames at different distances: one wide shot with the whole monument and its setting, then a closer one of the horses. The monument is lit in the evening, so it is worth a second visit if you are nearby at dusk.
text.geographic_location: The monument stands in the open, tree-lined square of Place des Quinconces, in Bordeaux.
text.directions_text: From there the monument is about 1 minute on foot to the south-east, so you can also walk closer for detail shots. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide (0.5x) to take in the whole monument, the square and the trees. Then use the default lens (1x) for a natural-looking view of the column and fountain. Use the telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for close shots of the bronze horses and sculptures.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand in Place des Quinconces (north side of the monument). The column, the bronze horses and sculptures of the fountain, framed by the open square and trees. From there the monument lies to the south-east. You see the column, the bronze horses and the fountain sculptures framed by the open square and trees.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and put the column on a vertical line, keeping the phone level so it does not lean. Keep the fountain's sculptures in the lower part of the frame and leave some open square and tree branches around them. If you want a different view, the Quai Louis XVIII shows the monument in the distance with the Garonne in front. One guide suggests the Pont de Pierre can frame the monument through the stone arches of the bridge.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the monument to focus, then lower the exposure slider a little so the sky does not turn white. In the evening, when the monument is lit, try night mode and hold the phone steady against your body or a railing. Live Photos can catch movement if the fountain is running.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early morning gives soft light and fewer people. In the evening, once the monument is illuminated, it makes a good second visit.

text.access_note: This is an open public square, and the viewpoint is free. Fairs and events can crowd or block views, so you may need to move to find a clear angle.

name: Musée d'Aquitaine
label: Musée d'Aquitaine
camera_source: No separate stand-here point: photographed at the spot itself (indoors, from its top, or right in front of it); drawn as the split pin.
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/80024893: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Musée d'Aquitaine' (143 m across).
notes: History museum of Bordeaux and Aquitaine.

text.description:
The Musée d'Aquitaine is Bordeaux's history museum, with more than 70,000 pieces that follow the story of the city and the region from Prehistory to today. Its collections include the Venus of Laussel, a Gallic gold torque and the cenotaph of Michel de Montaigne. There are also around 5,000 works from Africa and Oceania, which reflect the city's port history.

The building is part of the appeal. It was put up in the 1880s by the municipal architect Charles Durand as the Faculty of Letters and Sciences, on the site of older convents. The museum moved in on 9 January 1987. The outline on the map is about 143 m across, so this is a big, broad building. It is a good subject for a straightforward travel photo showing the long front with some of the surrounding street in the frame.

The museum sits in the centre of Bordeaux, close to Tour Pey-Berland and the cathedral. That makes it easy to combine with other photos in the same area. For the best result, take a few steps back so the whole width fits, keep your phone level, and check that vertical lines stay straight. If you plan to photograph inside, rules on photography can differ from room to room, so ask at the desk.
text.geographic_location: In the centre of Bordeaux, close to Tour Pey-Berland and Saint-André Cathedral.
text.directions_text: Head for the centre of Bordeaux and the area around Tour Pey-Berland and the cathedral; the museum is close by. Line B of the Bordeaux tramway serves a station called Musée d'Aquitaine. The phone icon on the map is at the subject itself. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide (0.5x) for the full width of the building, then switch to the default lens (1x) for a more natural look. If your phone has a 2x-5x telephoto, use it for details such as windows or stonework.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand right at the subject: the phone icon on the map marks the spot. To photograph the front, move out to the edge of the building and look back at it. Stepping further back gives you the whole width.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and line up the edges of the building with the vertical lines so it does not lean. Keep the phone level and at chest height. Use the ultra-wide only if you can keep the building in the centre of the frame, because the sides can stretch near the edges.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the building to focus, then slide the exposure down a little if the sky looks washed out. Try a quick panorama if you cannot step far enough back.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Daylight is easiest for the exterior. A softer, lower sun in the morning or late afternoon usually gives the stonework more shape.

name: Bordeaux Cathedral
label: Cathédrale St-André
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Place Pey-Berland' (2 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Place Pey Berland' (relation/4741796): middle (270 m across).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/80181137: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Cathédrale Saint-André' (145 m across).
notes: Gothic cathedral with a separate bell tower.

text.description: Bordeaux Cathedral, officially the Cathedral of St Andrew, is a big Gothic church with a tall, separate bell tower standing beside it. That pairing is what makes it so easy to photograph. From the square in front you can fit the carved stone façade, the tower and the everyday city around them into one frame, with people and tram lines in the foreground to give a sense of scale. A church of Saint-André is first recorded here in 814, and the earlier Romanesque church was consecrated in 1096. In 1137 Eleanor of Aquitaine married the future Louis VII of France in the cathedral. The Gothic rebuilding came later, and the bell tower was begun in 1440 and finished in 1500. UNESCO also lists the cathedral among the Bordeaux churches on the Routes of Santiago de Compostela. For a phone photo, the open square gives you a clean background and room to step back. Keep your phone upright so the walls don't lean, switch on the gridlines to help, and wait for a gap between passers-by or trams. A second, quieter angle is from Place Rohan, where the façade stands across from the Palais Rohan.
text.geographic_location: In the historic centre of Bordeaux, on the east side of Place Pey-Berland, with its separate bell tower right beside it. Place Rohan, in front of the Palais Rohan, is close by.
text.directions_text: Head for Place Pey-Berland in the centre of Bordeaux. Trams run through the square, so look both ways before crossing. For the alternative view, go to nearby Place Rohan next to the Palais Rohan. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) to get the whole façade and the bell tower in one frame. If you can't fit it all in, switch to the ultra-wide (0.5x) rather than walking into the tram lines. Use the telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for details of the stonework and the top of the tower.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand in Place Pey-Berland (in front of the west façade, facing the cathedral). The full Gothic façade with the separate Pey-Berland bell tower beside it, with tram lines and people in the foreground. The cathedral lies to the east, straight ahead of you. From here the photo shows the full Gothic façade with the separate Pey-Berland bell tower beside it, and tram lines and people in the foreground. Guides name this as the spot for a full-façade shot.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Switch on the gridlines and hold the phone level, without tilting it upwards, so the walls stay straight. Place the façade in the middle and leave a strip of square and tram lines at the bottom for depth. If you want people in the picture, wait until someone walks into that strip. For a quieter alternative, try Place Rohan, where the façade stands across from the Palais Rohan.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the stone façade to set focus, then drag the exposure slider down slightly if the sky looks washed out. Check the tram lines before you step back to frame the shot.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early evening, when warm light falls on the stone.

text.access_note: The outside can be photographed from open public squares, but the cathedral is a place of worship and the tower climb is paid, so check the official site before you go; photography inside is allowed without flash, but not during Mass.
claims_not_in_sources: Ultra-wide shots can make walls appear to lean if the phone is tilted upwards.
Place Rohan is quieter than Place Pey-Berland.
Dropping the exposure slightly helps when the sky is bright behind the stonework.

name: Place des Quinconces
label: Place des Quinconces
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Quai Louis XVIII' (2 web pages); placed at the stretch of Quai Louis XVIII nearest the subject (our map tiles).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap relation/5240389: 'Monument aux Girondins', the best-known feature inside 'Esplanade des Quinconces' (388 m across).
notes: One of the largest city squares in Europe.

text.description: Place des Quinconces is one of the largest city squares in Europe, about 25.6 hectares of open space between the centre of Bordeaux and the Garonne. It was laid out in 1820 on the site of the old Château Trompette, and the trees were planted in 1818 in staggered rows called quincunxes, which gave the square its name. That wide, open space is the reason it photographs well. Gravel, tree lines and sky leave plenty of room, and the monuments rise out of it. The tallest is the 54-metre Monument aux Girondins, built between 1894 and 1902. It has a column topped by a figure of Liberty and bronze fountains with sea horses at its foot. Two 21-metre rostral columns, put up in 1829, stand at the river end of the square. The fountain's statues were removed in 1942, then recovered, restored and re-erected in 1983. For a calmer picture than the usual central view, take the riverside promenade on Quai Louis XVIII and look back at the square. From there you see the whole tree-lined expanse, with the monument small and far away at the end of it. If you want the sculpture in detail, walk into the square and shoot the monument and fountain from close by.
text.geographic_location: The square lies between the river and the city centre, with the large theatre on one side.
text.directions_text: Start from the centre of Bordeaux and head for the Garonne riverbank, east of the square, and go to Quai Louis XVIII on the riverside promenade. If you are already at the square, walk east to the river from the Monument aux Girondins. That is about 5 minutes on foot. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) to show the whole square. Switch to telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) to bring the monument closer. Use the ultra-wide (0.5x) only if you stand much nearer the rostral columns.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand on Quai Louis XVIII (riverside promenade on the Garonne bank, east of the square, facing west toward it). The square seen from the river edge, with the tree-lined expanse and the monument set back in the distance. Face west toward the square, with the Monument aux Girondins straight ahead across the open space.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and put the monument on one of the vertical lines, with the tree lines leading toward it. Keep the horizon level. Leave plenty of sky above the column. If you want the sculpture up close, a second option is to shoot the monument and its fountain from within the square.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the monument to set focus, then slide the exposure down a little so the sky keeps its colour. Try a 2x or 3x shot, and take a panorama to capture the full width of the square.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Morning is likely to be easiest, with the sun behind you as you face west. In the evening you will be shooting toward the light. Rides, a Ferris wheel, circus tents or a Christmas market may occupy the square in some seasons, so check what is there when you arrive.

text.access_note: Rides, a Ferris wheel, circus tents or a Christmas market may occupy the square in some seasons and block the view, so check what is there when you arrive.
claims_not_in_sources: Facing west from the riverbank puts the morning sun behind the photographer and the evening sun in front of them.
A Ferris wheel, funfair, circus tents or Christmas market can occupy the square in some seasons and block the view.
From the monument it is about 5 minutes on foot to the riverbank viewpoint (calculated from the distance to the stand-here point).

name: Pont de pierre
label: Pont de pierre
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Quai de Queyries' (2 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Quai des Queyries' (node/13146018863): point.
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap node/5681165723: the OpenStreetMap point 'Pont de pierre'.
notes: Napoleonic stone bridge with 17 arches over the Garonne.

text.description: The Pont de pierre is the old brick-built bridge that carries Bordeaux across the Garonne. It was the city's first bridge, built between 1819 and 1822, and it is 487 m long with 17 arches. Despite the name, it is built mainly of brick, with pale medallions along the piers. That long, repeating row of arches is what makes it work so well on a phone: it gives you a strong line across the frame, with the river below and the sky above. From there you look back along the whole run of arches, with the spire of the Saint-Michel basilica rising beyond the far end. Two other spots are worth a try if the quay is busy. Quai Richelieu frames the bridge with the old quayside façades. Jardin des Lumières shows it as a thin horizon line and is usually quieter. The bridge is being renovated over several years, so you may find scaffolding, fencing or temporary cycle and pedestrian lanes in some views. Walk a little along the quay to find a cleaner angle. Keep the horizon level, and wait for a tram or a cyclist to cross if you want a sense of scale.
text.geographic_location: The bridge crosses the Garonne in Bordeaux, joining cours Victor Hugo on the left bank to the Bastide district (Avenue Thiers) on the right bank.
text.directions_text: There is no tram or railway stop right at this spot, so head for the Bastide district on the right bank of the Garonne. Quai de Queyries runs along the river there. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) to fit the whole row of arches in one frame. Try the telephoto (2x-3x, depending on your phone) to bring the Saint-Michel spire closer behind the bridge. The ultra-wide (0.5x) is best saved for the closer quayside viewpoints.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand on Quai de Queyries (right bank (rive droite) of the Garonne, looking back at the bridge). The full run of the bridge's arches across the river, with the Saint-Michel basilica spire visible beyond the far end. On the right bank (rive droite) of the Garonne, and look back at the bridge. From here you see the full run of arches across the river, with the Saint-Michel basilica spire beyond the far end.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Switch on the gridlines and place the bridge along the lower third, with the sky above and its reflection in the river below. Keep the spire clear of the bridge's edge, and move a few steps along the quay if fencing or scaffolding gets in the way. If the quay is busy or the works are in the way, Quai Richelieu (bridge framed by historic façades) and Jardin des Lumières (bridge as a horizon line) are good alternatives.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the bridge to set focus, then lower the exposure slider slightly so the sky keeps its colour. After dark, use night mode and rest your elbows on something steady, such as a railing, to keep the lights sharp.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Sunrise and sunset give soft light from the riverbanks. Early morning is also likely to be quieter on the quay.

text.access_note: The quay and riverbank are open public space, but the bridge is under renovation, so check the official site before you go for any closures or diversions.

name: Basilica of St. Michael
label: Basilique St-Michel
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Place Meynard' (2 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Place Meynard' (relation/5620926): middle (159 m across).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/116379269: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Basilique Saint-Michel' (94 m across).
notes: Gothic basilica with the tallest bell tower in southern France.

text.description:
The Basilica of St Michael is a Flamboyant Gothic church at the heart of Bordeaux's old Saint-Michel quarter. It was built between the end of the 14th century and the 16th century. Its most striking feature is the separate bell tower, 114 metres tall and built in the 15th century, which stands apart from the church and dominates the skyline. The church is on the Inventory of Historic Monuments and is part of the Santiago de Compostela pilgrim routes World Heritage listing, along with two other Bordeaux churches.

From this side the tall bell tower rises above the open space, and it photographs best as a dark, dramatic silhouette against a bright sky. The tower is too tall to fit in a normal upright shot at close range, so work with the space you have: step back, tilt the phone upwards and keep the edges of the frame tidy. If you want a different view, the Pont de Pierre and the Quai des Salinières both show the basilica and its tower from across the Garonne. The bridge arches and river make a good foreground. Wherever you stand, take a moment to straighten the phone so the tower does not lean.
text.geographic_location: The basilica is in the old Saint-Michel quarter of Bordeaux. Place Meynard is the square beside it.
text.directions_text: Head for the Saint-Michel quarter. Make for Place Meynard, the square next to the basilica. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the tower and square together. Switch to ultra-wide (0.5x) if you want more of the square and the church, and use telephoto (2x-5x) to pick out details near the top of the tower.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand in Place Meynard. The bell tower rising over the square, photographed as a dramatic silhouette. From here the bell tower rises over the open space, and it makes a strong silhouette.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and line the tower up with a vertical grid line. Hold the phone as level as you can, because tilting it upwards makes the tower lean. Include a little of the square at the bottom for scale. For a river view with the bridge arches in the foreground, try the Pont de Pierre instead.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the bright sky to set focus and exposure, then drag the exposure slider down a little. The tower will turn into a clean dark silhouette.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Golden hour, when the low light gives the sky colour behind the tower.

text.access_note: Place Meynard is an open public square, but the basilica is a place of worship. The bell tower can be visited from April to October, so check before you go if you plan to climb it.

name: Tour Pey-Berland
label: Tour Pey-Berland
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Place Pey Berland' (3 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Place Pey Berland' (relation/4741796): middle (270 m across).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/79978925: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Tour Pey Berland' (20 m across).
notes: Bell tower with a climbable viewpoint over the city.

text.description: The Tour Pey-Berland is the separate bell tower of Bordeaux Cathedral, and it stands right beside it on Place Pey Berland. It was built between 1440 and 1500 on the initiative of Archbishop Pey Berland, and it was kept apart from the cathedral so the vibrations of the bells would not harm the main building. Its tall, slim shape with a crowning steeple suits a portrait-format phone photo, and the open square in front gives you room to step back and fit the whole height in. The cathedral stands next to it, so you can also frame the two together. The tower has had an unusual past. It was used as housing until 1790, then as a lead factory, and its bells were only installed after 1851. Visitors can climb 230 steps to a panoramic view, but that is a separate timed visit with limited numbers, so check current opening. This spot is about the ground-level views. For a different angle, walk up Rue du Loup and look toward the spire between the facades on either side. Or go down to Quai Richelieu, where the tower can be seen with the Garonne in the foreground. Keep your phone upright, stand square-on to the tower so the sides do not lean, and give the sky some space above the spire.
text.geographic_location: In the centre of Bordeaux, on Place Pey Berland, immediately next to Bordeaux Cathedral (Saint-André).
text.directions_text: Make your way to Place Pey Berland on foot or by any local transport that suits you. From there the tower lies to the east, about 150 m away and roughly 2 minutes on foot. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide (0.5x) to fit the whole tower from the square, then try the default lens (1x) for a more natural look. Use telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) to pick out the stonework and the steeple.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand in Place Pey Berland. The tower rising from the square, seen from the ground in front of the adjacent cathedral, which is the classic full-height shot. For the close-up view, walk east from there to the square in front of the cathedral, next to the tower. From the square the tower rises above you and you get the classic full-height shot.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn the phone upright and switch on the gridlines. Place the tower on one of the vertical lines, keep the sides of the phone parallel to the tower to limit leaning, and leave a little sky above the steeple. Include part of the cathedral for context. If you want something different, shoot up Rue du Loup toward the spire, or from Quai Richelieu with the Garonne in front.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the sky or the tower to set focus, then drag the exposure slider down slightly so the sky keeps its colour and the stone keeps its detail. With the ultra-wide lens, keep people out of the extreme corners, where faces can look stretched.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Late afternoon is recommended for golden light on the tower. Early morning is also a good time to visit if you want the square quieter.

text.access_note: The square is an open public space, but climbing the tower is a timed, limited-number visit, so check the official site before you go for opening and any closures.

name: Jardin Public
label: Jardin Public
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Jardin botanique de Bordeaux' (2 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Jardin Botanique' (way/25674919): edge nearest the subject (662 m across).
pin_note: Position from OSM W21025479 (Jardin Public): kept: no OpenStreetMap object carries this Wikidata ID.
notes: Landscaped park north of the centre.

text.description:
The Jardin Public is a city park in Bordeaux, and it suits a phone camera because it gives you three quite different pictures within one visit: a wide green view, a formal terrace and a quiet pond.

From this side you can take a wide view across the park with the greenhouses in the background. It is a calmer alternative to the terrace, and guides recommend pairing this side with the greenhouses as a backdrop.

The second picture is the Terrasse du Jardin public: a long formal terrace with flower beds, statues and a building along one edge, and the basin in front. Stand back far enough to get the basin in the foreground and let the flower beds lead the eye towards the building.

The third is from the Petit Pont, the small footbridge over the pond. Here you can photograph the tree-lined banks, with swans and ducks on the water. The pond boat may not be running, so don't plan a shot around it.

Use these spots as a guide and walk a little until the view matches. Keep the phone level, use the gridlines, and take a few frames of each scene so you can choose later.
text.geographic_location: The Jardin Public is a city park in Bordeaux.
text.directions_text: Walk west and let the terrace and pond come into view. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the wide view across the park. Switch to ultra-wide (0.5x) on the terrace, and to telephoto/zoom (2x or more, depending on your phone) for statues and the swans.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand in Jardin botanique de Bordeaux (botanical garden side of the park). A wide view across the park from the botanical garden side, with greenhouses in the background. For the alternatives, use the Terrasse du Jardin public for the flower beds, statues and basin, or the Petit Pont for the pond.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: From the botanical garden side, put some lawn or planting in the foreground and place the greenhouses in the background, with the horizon on a gridline. On the terrace, keep the basin in the foreground and the building along one edge. From the Petit Pont, frame the tree-lined banks and wait for the swans or ducks to drift into the gap.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Turn on gridlines to keep the horizon straight. Tap on the main subject to focus, then drag the exposure slider down slightly if the sky is bright, so the greenery doesn't wash out. For the swans, try a Live Photo and pick the best frame afterwards.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: As general advice, soft morning or late-afternoon light usually flatters the greenery and the water.

text.access_note: This is a public park, but check the official site before you go for opening arrangements and any restrictions on parts of the garden.

name: Palais Rohan
label: Palais Rohan
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Place Pey-Berland' (3 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Place Pey Berland' (relation/4741796): middle (270 m across).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap relation/1203269: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Palais Rohan' (139 m across).
notes: Bordeaux's city hall in an 18th-century palace.

text.description:
The Palais Rohan is Bordeaux's City Hall, and it looks the part: a calm, pale stone neoclassical front with a clock set in the pediment above the central bays. It was built as the archbishop's palace. Archbishop Ferdinand Maximilien Mériadec de Rohan commissioned it in 1771 to replace an older medieval residence, and it was finished in 1778. The main building is three storeys high and stands at the back of a courtyard, with single-storey wings either side and an arcaded screen at the front. Napoleon and Louis XVIII both used it as a residence, and it became the city hall in 1835. It has been a protected historic monument since 1997.

It photographs well because the symmetry is so clear. The row of tall windows, the pilasters and the central pediment line up neatly on a phone screen, and the open square gives you room to step back and get the whole front in. The best-known view is from Place Pey-Berland, facing the palace across the square, with the cathedral close by. For a closer, more detailed picture, the courtyard shows the grand portal and ironwork gate. The garden behind shows the rear elevation. The main gate has been replaced after damage, so recent photos may look different from older ones. Interior photography is restricted, so plan on the exterior and courtyard. Temporary event stands can sometimes block the square.
text.geographic_location: The Palais Rohan is in central Bordeaux, on Place Pey-Berland, facing the cathedral. The city hall garden lies behind it.
text.directions_text: Head for Place Pey-Berland in the historic centre of Bordeaux. Walk towards it to reach the courtyard gate. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the front-on postcard shot, which takes in the whole facade and the open square. Use the telephoto (2x or more, depending on your phone) to pick out the clock and pediment. In the courtyard or the garden, where you are close to the building, switch to the ultra-wide (0.5x).
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand in Place Pey-Berland (across the square from the main front, with the cathedral nearby). The Louis XVI main facade with its central pediment and clock, framed by the open square. The palace is to the west of you. From here the photo shows the Louis XVI facade with its central pediment and clock, framed by the open square, with the cathedral nearby.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and line the central pediment up with the middle of the frame, keeping the phone level so the vertical lines stay straight. Leave a little empty square in the foreground to give a sense of scale. For a closer alternative, step into the Cour d'honneur for the portal and ironwork grille, or go round to the Jardin de la Mairie for the rear elevation with garden trees in front.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the facade to set focus, then slide the exposure down a touch if the pale stone or sky looks washed out. Keep Live Photos off in busy moments, or use it to catch people crossing the square. In the courtyard, hold the phone level when using the ultra-wide, or the edges will lean.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Late afternoon, when one photo guide says the facade gets warm light.

text.access_note: The square and the exterior are open public space, but the interior is open only on certain days and photography inside is restricted, so check the official site before you go.
claims_not_in_sources: Place Pey-Berland is an open public square that can be visited at any time.
Pale stone can look washed out in bright light, so lowering the exposure slider slightly may help.

name: Grand Théâtre de Bordeaux
label: Grand Théâtre
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Place de la Comédie' (3 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Place de la Comédie' (way/23247161): middle (102 m across).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/79734107: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Grand Théâtre' (104 m across).
notes: Neoclassical opera house with a columned facade.

text.description:
The Grand Théâtre is Bordeaux's opera house, and its front is made for a phone photo. A row of twelve tall Corinthian columns carries a stone ledge, and on top of that stand twelve statues: the nine Muses and three goddesses (Juno, Venus and Minerva). The architect was Victor Louis, and the theatre opened on 17 April 1780. It was planned as a temple to the arts, and the calm, symmetrical neoclassical front shows that. Today it is home to the Opéra National de Bordeaux and the Ballet National de Bordeaux.

The classic view is from Place de la Comédie, the open square in front. The space lets you fit the whole facade in, and a passing tram adds some life and movement to the picture. Standing towards the right-hand side of the building, near the tram stop, gives a more flattering angle than straight on. Take one shot of the full front, then wait for a tram to cross the frame and take another.

For a more personal picture, ask a friend to stand on the steps with the columns behind them. If the square is busy, the Allées de Tourny, the tree-lined avenue, offers a framed view of the theatre with fewer people. Late afternoon is lovely, and the lit-up facade after dark is also worth a few minutes.
text.geographic_location: The theatre stands in the centre of Bordeaux, facing Place de la Comédie, the square at its front.
text.directions_text: Head for Place de la Comédie in the centre of Bordeaux; by taxi or hired scooter, ask for the Grand Théâtre. No station or tram stop name is given for this spot, so use the tram stop beside the square as a landmark once you are there. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) from the square for the whole facade. Switch to ultra-wide (0.5x) if you are close and the columns are cut off, and use telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for the statues along the top.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand in Place de la Comédie (front of the theatre facade, right-hand side near the tram stop). The full neoclassical facade with its twelve corinthian columns and the statues of the Muses, framed by the open square and passing tram. Stand towards the right-hand side of the facade, near the tram stop, with the theatre to the east of you. From here you see all twelve columns and the statues of the Muses, framed by the open square and any passing tram.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and line the columns up with the vertical lines so the building doesn't lean. Keep the full width of the facade in the frame, with some square at the bottom for scale. Take a second shot when a tram passes. For a variation, try the Allées de Tourny for a view down the tree-lined avenue.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the stonework to set focus, then drag the exposure slider down slightly so the sky stays blue and the columns keep their detail. Use portrait mode for a person on the steps. After dark, use night mode and hold the phone steady against something solid.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Late afternoon or golden hour, when low light picks out the columns and statues. The illuminated facade after dark is also recommended.

text.access_note: The square in front is open public space, but the interior is visited by guided tour only, so check the official site before you go and look out for event closures on the square.
claims_not_in_sources: Trams run past the front of the theatre, so a tram can often be caught in the frame.
The Allées de Tourny view is usually less crowded than the square.
The facade is lit up after dark.
Event-related closures of Place de la Comédie can happen.

name: Basilica of Saint Severinus
label: Basilique St-Seurin
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Place des Martyrs-de-la-Résistance' (2 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Place des Martyrs de la Résistance' (way/191079279): middle (139 m across).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/154853572: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Basilique Saint-Seurin' (98 m across).
notes: Ancient basilica with a Romanesque portal.

text.description: Saint Severinus (Saint-Seurin in French) is one of the three Bordeaux churches that share a UNESCO World Heritage listing as part of the Routes of Santiago de Compostela in France. It was rebuilt as a sturdy Romanesque church from the early 11th century, on ground that was a Christian burial place as far back as the 4th century. It photographs well because the square in front gives you room to step back and fit the whole west-to-south side into one frame: the 19th-century neo-Romanesque west front, the old bell tower beside it, and the porch with its belfry on the south side. The south side also has a 13th-century Gothic entrance decorated with fourteen carved figures, so there is plenty of detail if you want a closer shot. Look for the statues on the west front too, including Saint Severinus and Saint Amand, whose meeting is shown above the door. The church was listed as a historic monument in 1840. Take your main shot from the landscaped square. A gentle zoom picks out the tower and carvings without you needing to move. If you have time, Rue Rodrigue, the street behind the basilica, may give a closer view of the south portal and side walls, so check on the day. The church may be closed inside after a fire in the sacristy, but the outside views are not affected.
text.geographic_location: The basilica stands on Place des Martyrs-de-la-Résistance in Bordeaux. The landscaped square lies directly in front of the church.
text.directions_text: No tram or railway stop is listed for this spot, so start from the centre of Bordeaux and go by taxi or hired scooter, asking for Place des Martyrs-de-la-Résistance, the basilica's address. From there the basilica is to the north, about 1 minute on foot. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide (0.5x) to fit the whole facade and bell tower in. Switch to the default lens (1x) for a more natural look, then to the telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for the tower top and the carved details.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand in Place des Martyrs-de-la-Résistance. The west-to-south facade and bell tower of the basilica, seen across the landscaped square in front of the church. From here you see the west-to-south facade and the bell tower across the landscaped square, with the basilica ahead of you to the north.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and line the tower up with a vertical line so it does not lean. Use the landscaped planting of the square as a foreground frame. As a closer alternative, Rue Rodrigue, behind the basilica, may give a closer view of the south portal and side walls, so check on the day.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the church wall to focus, then slide the exposure down a little so the pale stone keeps its detail against a bright sky. Hold the phone level, because tilting it up makes the tower lean inwards. If you use the ultra-wide, keep the church in the middle of the frame to limit edge stretching.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Choose a time when the sun is behind or beside you rather than over the tower. Check how the light falls when you arrive.

text.access_note: The outside can be photographed from the public square, but this is a place of worship that may be closed after a fire in the sacristy, so check the official site before you go if you want to go inside.

name: Church of the Holy Cross
label: Église Sainte-Croix
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Place Pierre Renaudel' (3 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Place Pierre Renaudel' (way/51429499): middle (126 m across).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/119060953: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Abbatiale Sainte-Croix' (79 m across).

text.description: The Church of the Holy Cross (Église Sainte-Croix) is a Romanesque church that once belonged to a Benedictine abbey founded in the 7th century. The building you see dates from the late 11th and early 12th centuries. It photographs well because the west front is so clearly composed: two square towers, a carved portal and richly sculpted stonework, all facing an open paved square. That space lets you step back and fit the whole façade in one frame. Inside, the nave is 39 m long and the apse is 15.30 m high. The church was restored in the 19th century by Paul Abadie, and the old abbey buildings now house the École des beaux-arts de Bordeaux. For the classic shot, stand in Place Pierre Renaudel and look at the façade straight on, using the paving as a foreground. Then step closer and use the zoom for the carvings around the doorway. If you have a few minutes, walk round to Square Dom-Bedos, a garden on the east side. From there you can photograph the rounded apse and side chapels, a quieter angle away from the main front. Works have sometimes fenced off parts of the square, so the view may be partly blocked on the day. Keep an eye out for passers-by, who can add a sense of scale if you wait for the right moment.
text.geographic_location: In Bordeaux, southern France, beside the former Benedictine abbey buildings that now house the École des beaux-arts de Bordeaux. The best view is from Place Pierre Renaudel, the square in front of the church's west façade.
text.directions_text: No tram or railway stop is listed for this spot, so head for Place Pierre Renaudel in Bordeaux by taxi or hired scooter. Square Dom-Bedos, the garden on the east side of the church, is a short walk round the building. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) to take in both towers and the portal. Use the ultra-wide (0.5x) if the square is crowded or you are close, and the telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for the carved doorway and sculpted details.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand in Place Pierre Renaudel (in front of the west façade). The Romanesque west front with its two square towers, carved portal and sculpted façade, framed across the open paved square. From here you look across the open paved square at the Romanesque west front with its two square towers, carved portal and sculpted stonework.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and line the centre of the portal up with the middle vertical line so both towers sit evenly either side. Hold the phone level so the towers do not lean. Keep a strip of paving at the bottom for depth. For a different view, try the rounded apse and side chapels from Square Dom-Bedos on the east side.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the pale stonework to focus, then lower the exposure slider a little so the carvings keep their detail and the sky does not wash out. If you use the ultra-wide (0.5x), keep the façade near the middle of the frame, because the edges can look stretched.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: The west front probably looks warmest in the afternoon or early evening, but any time with soft daylight works. Visiting when the square is quiet makes it easier to get a clear view of the façade.

text.access_note: The square is an open public space, but parts of it have been fenced off during works, the church is open only at certain times and Square Dom-Bedos may have limited hours, so check the official site before you go.

name: Pont Jacques Chaban-Delmas
label: Pont Chaban-Delmas
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Quai de Bacalan' (2 web pages); placed at the stretch of Quai de Bacalan nearest the subject (our map tiles).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/440836465: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Jacques Chaban-Delmas Bridge' (161 m across).

text.description:
The Pont Jacques Chaban-Delmas is a vertical-lift bridge over the Garonne. Its middle section is a deck that rises straight up between two tall pylons so ships can pass underneath. That shape is what makes it a good photo subject: two upright towers, a long flat deck and a wide stretch of river and sky behind them. It opened on 16 March 2013, and its main span is 110 m long. When it opened it was the longest vertical-lift bridge in Europe. It is named after Jacques Chaban-Delmas, a former Prime Minister of France and former mayor of Bordeaux.

The best-known angle is from the Bacalan bank of the river, at the bridge foot where the lifting section rises. From there the pylons and deck sit against the water, and you can include the river in the frame. If you want a second angle, the Quai de Brazza on the Bastide side shows the lifting span with reflections in the river. The Cité du Vin gives a higher, wider view of the bridge and the city, though you should check the official site before you go in case a ticket is needed for the viewing level.

Go in the morning or evening, when it is usually quieter. Check the bridge's lift schedule too: when the deck rises, traffic stops, and the timing changes when ships pass. A raised deck makes a very different picture from a lowered one, so it is worth waiting for if you have the time.
text.geographic_location: The bridge crosses the Garonne in Bordeaux, joining the Bacalan district on the left bank to the Bastide side on the right bank.
text.directions_text: No tram or railway stops are listed for this spot; head for the Quai de Bacalan on the left bank of the Garonne. Walk along the quay towards the bridge foot where the lifting section rises. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide (0.5x) to fit both pylons, the deck and the river into one frame. Switch to the default lens (1x) for a calmer, more natural view. Use telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for close shots of the pylons or the deck against the sky.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand on Quai de Bacalan (left (Bacalan) bank, at the bridge foot where the lift span rises). The pylons and lifting deck framed against the Garonne, with the river and sky behind the bridge. From here the bridge lies to the south-east, with the pylons and lifting deck framed against the Garonne and the sky behind. For the best-known view, walk a short way along the quay towards the bridge foot where the lift span rises.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and line up one pylon with a vertical grid line to keep the tower upright. Leave the river in the lower part of the frame and the sky above. For a different view, try the Quai de Brazza on the Bastide side, where the lifting span and its reflections in the river show well.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the sky or the bright part of the bridge to focus, then drag the exposure slider down a little so the sky keeps its colour and the pylons are not washed out. If the deck is about to lift, try a Live Photo or a short burst to catch the movement. After dark, use night mode and hold the phone steady against a rail or wall.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Morning or evening, which is usually quieter. Check the lift schedule before you go, as the deck rises when ships pass.

text.access_note: The Quai de Bacalan viewpoint is a public street by the river; check the official site before you go if you plan to use the Cité du Vin viewing level, as a ticket may be needed.
